headline: Moonvalley's Marey Gives Filmmakers Keyframe Control Over AI Camera
lede: A new feature from AI video startup Moonvalley lets creators choreograph precise camera movements — dollies, pans, arcs — applied to still images or existing footage. The tool, called Marey, is aimed at filmmakers who want cinematic control without surrendering to a model's best guess. Director Paul Trillo posted a demonstration showing the results.
body:
The central problem with most AI video generators is that the camera moves wherever the model decides. Prompt-based tools produce motion that is plausible but not directed — useful for rough ideation, frustrating for anyone with a specific shot in mind. Marey addresses this by letting the user set *keyframes*: explicit spatial positions the virtual camera must pass through at defined moments, with the model filling the motion between them.

Keyframing is the backbone of traditional animation and visual-effects work. An animator specifies where a camera — or character, or object — sits at frame 1 and frame 60; software interpolates the path between. Marey applies the same logic to AI-generated video, giving creators the vocabulary of conventional cinematography without the physical rig.

The feature works on both static images and existing video clips, which meaningfully expands its utility. A photograph can be given a slow push-in; a talking-head clip can have a subtle arc added in post. This places Marey in a growing category sometimes called *virtual camera movement* — AI that synthesises depth and parallax to simulate motion that was never physically captured.

Paul Trillo, a director whose work with AI video tools has attracted wide attention, posted the demonstration. His endorsement matters in this space: he has a track record of stress-testing these platforms seriously rather than showcasing cherry-picked outputs. The name Marey is almost certainly a nod to Étienne-Jules Marey, the 19th-century French physiologist who invented *chronophotography* — the technique of capturing motion across sequential frames, a direct ancestor of cinema itself. The homage is apt.

concepts.definition: A technique in animation and video production where a creator specifies the exact state of an object or camera at particular moments in time. Software then calculates and fills in the motion between those fixed points. It gives precise, repeatable control over movement.

AI-generated motion applied to a static image or footage clip to simulate the effect of a moving camera — zooms, pans, dollies — without any physical camera having moved. The model infers depth and parallax to make the synthesis look plausible.

A 19th-century photographic technique, pioneered by Étienne-Jules Marey and Eadweard Muybridge, that captured successive phases of motion in a single image or rapid sequence. It was foundational to the development of cinema and motion analysis.
